# Getting started

Renderizr renders a [Structurizr](https://structurizr.com/) workspace as a static site, or as a single self-contained HTML file you can host anywhere. The site holds every view, the workspace documentation and the decision log. This site is Renderizr's own architecture, rendered by Renderizr.

## Who it is for

You keep a C4 model in Structurizr, and you want everyone else to read it without an account, a running server or a copy of the DSL. Renderizr takes the workspace JSON you already have and turns it into pages you can put behind a URL. The engine draws each view from its workspace semantics: positions, styles, themes, shapes and routing. Diagrams read the way they do in Structurizr, with real text wrapping and embedded fonts.

Renderizr renders a workspace and leaves its definition to you: the model, the views and the styles all come from your workspace, unchanged.

## Requirements

- **Node 20 or newer.** The build checks the version before anything else and stops with a clear message, because `npx` runs whatever Node comes first on the `PATH`.
- **A workspace in JSON.** [structurizr-cli](https://docs.structurizr.com/cli) exports one from your DSL, and the Structurizr [server API](https://docs.structurizr.com/commands) hands one back. Renderizr never parses DSL.
- **Network access at build time**, only when the workspace, the logo or the font is remote, or when the workspace references themes or icons by URL. The rendered output never needs it.

Builds need nothing else: no JVM, no Docker, no Graphviz and no PlantUML. Only [edit mode](02-usage.md#edit-mode) on a `workspace.dsl` needs Structurizr's tools.

## Render a workspace

Point Renderizr at a workspace JSON file, by path or by URL. This command renders the Big Bank plc example:

```bash
npx github:FormulaMonks/renderizr https://raw.githubusercontent.com/structurizr/structurizr/main/structurizr-export/src/test/resources/big-bank-plc.json
```

Your own workspace works the same way:

```bash
npx github:FormulaMonks/renderizr ./workspace.json
```

The build takes a couple of seconds once npm has fetched the package, and writes the site into `./structurizr-output`: an `index.html`, an `assets/` folder and a favicon. The site uses relative URLs, so it works from any folder on any static host.

The site you are reading is Renderizr's own workspace, rendered this way. Every view gets a diagram that pans and zooms, listed down the side:

![The container view of Renderizr's workspace: the list of views on the left, the diagram and its controls on the right.](images/render-diagrams.png)

The documentation becomes pages, with a table of contents built from the headings:

![The Options section of the usage documentation: the table of contents on the left, the section's text and its flag table on the right.](images/render-documentation.png)

The decisions become a log, with a graph of the links between them:

![The decision log of Renderizr's workspace: each decision with its number and status, and a graph of its links to the others on the left.](images/render-decisions.png)

## Open the site

Serve the output folder with any static server:

```bash
npx servor structurizr-output
```

Then open the URL it prints. The views sit down the side; the header leads to the documentation and the decisions.

To open the result straight off your disk, or to send it to someone as one file, render with `--single-file` instead:

```bash
npx github:FormulaMonks/renderizr ./workspace.json --single-file
```

Then open `structurizr-output/index.html` in a browser. It needs no server and makes no network requests.

## What you get

- **Every view**, listed down the side: landscape, context, container, component, dynamic, deployment, image, filtered and custom, each with its own mark and key.
- **A live engine** built for workspace JSON. Diagrams pan and zoom, dynamic views animate, labels toggle, and an element with several activation targets opens a target menu.
- **Workspace documentation** as pages, with a table of contents and heading anchors. Heading ids match GitHub's, and relative links between documentation files and decisions open the matching page. Markdown gets GitHub-style alerts, permalinks and highlighting, images show from the copies Structurizr embeds in the workspace, and Renderizr converts AsciiDoc to the same pages.
- **The decision log**, with status pills, supersessions and amendments, grouped by year.
- **Light and dark**, following the reader's system setting until they choose one. The page and the diagrams keep separate preferences.
- **[Export](02-usage.md#export)** of any drawn view as an SVG or PNG file, framed by its canvas, with a title block below.
- **Deep links that last**: routing lives in the URL hash, so a link to a view, document or decision still works after a reload, over `file://` and inside a sandboxed frame.

Renderizr reads documentation and decisions from the workspace level (`documentation.sections` and `documentation.decisions`). It leaves out sections attached to an individual software system or container.

## License

Renderizr is MIT-licensed, copyright (c) 2024-2026 Monks Tech Services. Every rendered page bundles code Renderizr did not write: React and React Flow (MIT), Dagre (MIT), [Bootstrap Icons](https://icons.getbootstrap.com) (MIT) and the other libraries the page needs. Its model layer derives from Structurizr's own code (Apache 2.0). [THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md](https://github.com/FormulaMonks/renderizr/blob/main/THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md) lists each one with its version, license and copyright line, and says whether it ships in the output or only runs during the build. [NOTICE](https://github.com/FormulaMonks/renderizr/blob/main/NOTICE) is the short form.

## Next steps

- [Usage](02-usage.md) covers every flag, the single file, export, edit mode and using Renderizr from an AI agent.
- [Contributing](03-contributing.md) takes you from a clone to a merged pull request.
- [Reference](04-reference.md) covers local development, every pnpm script, Structurizr's tools for edit mode, the project layout and adding a test.

# Usage ```bash npx github:FormulaMonks/renderizr [options] npx github:FormulaMonks/renderizr edit [path] [options] ``` The first form renders a workspace. The second starts [edit mode](#edit-mode). `renderizr --help` and `renderizr edit --help` print the same reference as text. ## Options The one required argument is the workspace: a local path or an `http(s)` URL to a Structurizr workspace **JSON** file. Every flag is optional. ```bash npx github:FormulaMonks/renderizr ./workspace.json \ --single-file \ --logo ./logo.svg \ --font "Inter" ``` | Flag | Effect | | --- | --- | | `-o, --out ` | Output directory, relative to the current directory. Default `structurizr-output`. The build empties it first | | `--single-file` | Emit one self-contained `index.html` with every asset inlined, plus `artifact.html` | | `--base ` | Base public path for the multi-file build. The default is empty, which emits relative URLs (`./assets/…`) that work from any folder. Set it to a path such as `/renderizr/` when the page must reference its assets absolutely | | `--logo ` | Image at the top left of the header: a path relative to the current directory, a URL or a `data:` URI. The build fetches it, minifies it when it is SVG, and embeds it as a data URI. It recognizes PNG, JPEG, GIF, WebP and SVG from their bytes, and rejects an SVG that holds a script | | `--logo-alt ` | Alt text for the logo. Default empty. When it matches the workspace name, the logo stands in for the title in the header, so a logo that spells the name does not repeat it | | `--logo-href ` | Wraps the logo in a link | | `--font ` | A [Google Fonts](https://fonts.google.com) family, such as `Inter` or `"Source Sans 3"`. The build downloads it from Google Fonts, its one font source, as woff2 and embeds it, diagram labels included | | `--font-weights ` | Comma-separated weights. Default `400,700`. The build prefers a variable font that covers the range when the family has one | | `--font-subsets ` | Comma-separated subsets. Default `latin` | | `--font-italic` | Also embed the italic faces, which roughly doubles the font's weight | | `--primary-color ` | A CSS color, such as `#e4572e` or `rgb(228 87 46)`, for links, the active page and view, edit mode's marks and the nodes of a [Mermaid diagram](#mermaid-diagrams) whose source sets no theme, in light and dark alike. Default is Renderizr's blue | | `-h, --help` | Print the reference as text and exit | A font is the one option with a real cost: an embedded family outweighs every other option together, and each extra weight, subset or italic face adds to it. ## Branding from the workspace Set the logo, the font and the primary color once in the workspace, and every run of `renderizr` and `renderizr edit` uses them without flags: ``` workspace { properties { "renderizr.logo" "logo.svg" "renderizr.logoAlt" "Acme" "renderizr.logoHref" "https://acme.example" "renderizr.font" "Inter" "renderizr.primaryColor" "#e4572e" } } ``` | Property | Holds | Flag that overrides it | | --- | --- | --- | | `renderizr.logo` | The header logo: a path relative to the workspace file, or to the workspace URL when you render from one, a URL or a `data:` URI | `--logo` | | `renderizr.logoAlt` | The logo's alt text | `--logo-alt` | | `renderizr.logoHref` | The link around the logo | `--logo-href` | | `renderizr.font` | A Google Fonts family name, the value `--font` takes | `--font` | | `renderizr.primaryColor` | A CSS color | `--primary-color` | - A flag overrides its property for that run. When a run passes a flag whose value differs from the workspace, Renderizr prints a `properties` block to paste into the workspace, with a logo path relative to the workspace file. - Renderizr checks a property the way it checks its flag. An invalid value fails the build, or the start of edit mode, and the error names the property and the workspace. - Renderizr reads these properties and never writes them. It skips Structurizr's `branding` block, and prints a notice when that block sets a logo or a font that no property sets. - Edit mode applies branding when it starts. When you change a property while it runs, it asks you to restart `renderizr edit`. - `--font-weights`, `--font-subsets` and `--font-italic` have no properties yet. ## Default output Without `--single-file`, the build writes `index.html`, an `assets/` folder and a favicon. The files use relative URLs, so the site works from any folder of a static host such as GitHub Pages or S3. Use `--base` when a host needs absolute asset paths. The footer of every page says what is on screen and which Renderizr built it: a C4 view is in C4 notation and drawn with React Flow, a Mermaid diagram comes from Mermaid source and is drawn with React Flow, a picture names only the workspace, and the documentation and decisions pages say whose they are. ## Single file `--single-file` inlines every stylesheet, script, font, icon and the workspace itself into one document that makes no network requests at all: ```bash npx github:FormulaMonks/renderizr ./workspace.json --single-file ``` The build writes two files: | File | Use it for | | --- | --- | | `index.html` | Anywhere a URL can point: GitHub Pages, S3, an email attachment, or straight off your disk over `file://` | | `artifact.html` | Hosts that supply their own document scaffolding, such as a Claude artifact. It holds the same page without its own ``, `` or `` | Pick the single file when a folder of files is hard to hand over. One file goes in a chat message, an email, a wiki attachment or a bucket with no build step, and it opens off a USB stick on a machine with no network. The build fetches themes, element icons and a logo referenced by URL, and folds them all in. The page never reaches for the network, so it also works under a strict content security policy. ## Export Two buttons at the end of the diagram toolbar save the view on screen as a file: **Export view as PNG** and **Export view as SVG**. Every build has them, single file or not, and every view the engine draws has them, a [Mermaid diagram](#mermaid-diagrams) included; an image view that shows a picture has none. An export shows the view as drawn: the diagram color scheme, the animation step and the description and technology toggles the reader has on. The view's canvas frames it: its `dimensions`, else its paper size, else the content with 200 pixels of room on each side. A title block runs below the canvas, in the diagram's font and colors: 1. The view's title in bold, when it has one. 2. The view's description, wrapped to the canvas width and cut to four lines, when it has one. 3. "Author:" and the author the view's description names after `Author:`, email address included, else the workspace's `lastModifiedUser`, else its `lastModifiedAgent`. 4. "Last updated:" and the workspace's `lastModifiedDate`, else the date of the build, in the reader's locale. 5. "Created with Renderizr" and the version that built the site, smaller and lighter than the lines above it. Every export carries the author, date and credit lines. Each one prints "Unknown" only when neither the view nor the workspace gives it a value. The SVG keeps every label as real text and embeds the page's font, so it stays sharp at any size and fetches nothing. The PNG is twice the size of the SVG, and lowers its scale for a large canvas so it holds at most 16,777,216 pixels, which every browser can draw. The file takes the workspace's name and the view's key in kebab-case, then the step and the scheme when they apply: `big-bank-plc-system-context.png` for the full view in light, `big-bank-plc-sign-in-step-2-dark.svg` for step 2 of a dynamic view in dark. While an export runs, its button shows busy; when one fails, the toolbar says "Couldn't export this view". In edit mode, an export shows the layout as you left it, saved or not, without the selection, guides or canvas fill. Inside a Claude artifact, the page saves an export through the artifact viewer's `downloads` capability, which asks the reader to confirm each file. A save the reader declines ends quietly. An artifact published without `downloads` can't save a file, so its toolbar shows no export buttons: declare `downloads` when you publish `artifact.html`. An element icon given as an `http(s)` URL stays blank in an export. A build embeds every icon in the page, so this only happens on the dev server, which leaves such icons as URLs. ## Mermaid diagrams Renderizr draws a Mermaid flowchart, ERD or sequence diagram that an image view carries as a **Mermaid diagram**, in the workspace's font and color scheme, with the zoom, fit, color scheme and export buttons every view has. Write it the way Structurizr reads it, with the `mermaid` keyword, and change nothing else in the DSL: ``` views { properties { "mermaid.url" "https://mermaid.ink" } image * "order-flow" { mermaid order-flow.mmd title "Order flow" } } ``` Structurizr encodes the source into the image view's content as a URL on the Mermaid server that `mermaid.url` names, on the image view or on the views. The build reads the source back from that URL and parses it with Mermaid's own grammar, so the page never fetches the Mermaid server's picture. The workspace keeps opening in Structurizr as before. A source that opens with `flowchart`, `graph`, `erDiagram` or `sequenceDiagram` draws. Every other image view stays a picture with no warning: a picture file, Mermaid that Structurizr inlines with `mermaid.inline true`, and every other Mermaid type. Renderizr's own architecture carries one of each, under `architecture/mermaid/`: a flowchart of how the build reads an image view, an ERD of the layout data Structurizr keeps in `workspace.json`, and a sequence diagram of how edit mode saves a layout and draws a DSL session again. The view's `title` names the diagram, then the source's frontmatter `title`, then `Image View: `. The frontmatter title never draws on the canvas. In edit mode a Mermaid diagram draws read-only, since Structurizr keeps no layout for an image view, and a DSL session draws it again when its `.mmd` file under the DSL's folder changes. > [!TIP] > Choose every color on purpose, and give it a meaning. The C4 model asks that a diagram's colors say something, and so Renderizr derives its whole palette from one primary color. Renderizr honors a Mermaid source's own styles, and a source draws at its best when it sets none: with no `theme`, `themeVariables`, `classDef` or `style`, the diagram takes the workspace's primary color and styles, and reads like the C4 views beside it. Give a node a color of its own when the reader needs to tell it apart, and say what the color means in the view's description. A diagram Renderizr can't draw shows why in place of the canvas, and the build prints the same text and finishes: `Mermaid diagram "order-flow": a parse error at line 4: the source ends too early.` Its export buttons show disabled and say "Nothing to export: the diagram couldn't be drawn". In edit mode the reason shows on the view and in the terminal, and the next save of the source that fixes it draws the diagram again. [Mermaid diagram notices](04-reference.md#mermaid-diagram-notices) lists every reason. The description and technology toggles hide on a flowchart, whose labels hold the source's text alone. On an ERD the description toggle shows and hides the attributes' comment column, on the canvas and in an export, and the technology toggle hides, since an ERD has no technologies. A toggle that hides keeps your choice, which applies again on the next view where it shows. ### Flowcharts Renderizr lays a flowchart out with Dagre, the way Mermaid does at Renderizr's larger text: every length Mermaid uses grows by 1.5. Nodes sit 75 apart, ranks 75 apart and edges 30 apart, and a source's own `nodeSpacing` and `rankSpacing` grow the same way. Each node takes the size its label needs. A subgraph that no edge crosses lays out on its own and turns its direction (top to bottom becomes left to right) unless it sets `direction`. Every other subgraph stays part of the graph around it. ![The flowchart of how the build reads an image view, drawn in Renderizr's primary color: decisions as diamonds, with Yes and No edges to an ordinary image view, a ViewError or a Mermaid diagram.](images/mermaid-flowchart.png) | Source | Draws as | | --- | --- | | `A[text]`, `A(text)`, `A{text}`, `A((text))`, `A[(text)]`, `A{{text}}` | A rectangle, a rounded rectangle, a diamond, a circle, a cylinder and a hexagon | | `
` in a label | A new line | | `-->`, `-.->` and `==>` | A solid line, a dotted line and a line about twice as thick, with an arrow | | `---` | A solid line with no arrow | | `--o` and `--x` | A line ending in a filled circle and in a cross | | `<-->`, `o--o` and `x--x` | The same marker at both ends, on any line: `<-.->`, `o==o` | | `subgraph … end` | A group around its nodes | Every other shape falls back to a rectangle and warns: stadium, subroutine, asymmetric, parallelogram, trapezoid, double circle and every other `@{ shape }` name. An invisible link (`~~~`) draws nothing and leaves the layout, a longer link (`--->`) lays out as an ordinary one, and Markdown strings and `fa:` icons draw their text plain; each of them warns. End markers take the edge's color and draw solid on a dotted line, sized to the line as the arrow is. Each end with a marker leaves its node straight before the line may turn, and ranks sit far enough apart for the markers of a thick line to fit. A flowchart that Structurizr writes from a C4 view with `mermaid ` draws as any flowchart. The HTML in its labels draws as plain text lines. #### Click links A `click` line that gives a node a link, `click A href "#orders"` or `click A "https://example.com/shop"`, makes the node an activation target, the way an element link does. The link reads as an element link reads: `#`, `?view=` and `{workspace}/diagrams#` open that view, a page on Structurizr's own hosts opens the matching view or document here when the workspace has it, and any other address opens in a new tab. A link to the view on screen, to a view the workspace doesn't have or to a script offers nothing and warns about nothing. A tooltip after the link, `click A "https://example.com/shop" "Open the shop"`, shows when the pointer rests on the node. A node with a link draws the indicator for where it leads under its label and grows to fit it, joins the Tab order in reading order, and exports with its indicator. Subgraphs and edges never lead anywhere. A `click` line that calls a function, `click A callback` or `click A call notify()`, does nothing and warns, since the page runs no script from the source. In edit mode nothing activates, as on every view. #### Styles A flowchart's styles layer from the least specific to the most: the color scheme's defaults, then the workspace's tag styles with the themes they come from, then the source's config (a named `theme` or `themeVariables`), then its classes (`classDef default` first, then each `classDef` in the order the source defines it), then its own `style` and `linkStyle`. The workspace's element styles tagged `Element` and `Mermaid` apply to every node, its relationship styles tagged `Relationship` and `Mermaid` to every edge, and its element styles tagged `Group` and `Mermaid` to every subgraph. A `classDef` name isn't a tag. A node's `fontSize` applies unless the source sets a font size; its `width`, `height` and `shape` never do, since the source sets them. The shape and the line style that the arrow syntax sets always win. A source with no `theme` and no `themeVariables` takes the workspace's look. Its nodes fill with the primary color (`--primary-color`, then `renderizr.primaryColor`, then Renderizr's blue) with white text and a darker border, beneath the workspace's styles, in light and dark alike, and its edges and subgraphs take the color scheme's defaults. A source that names a `theme` or sets `themeVariables` takes the palette that Mermaid's own theme code derives from them, so a lone `primaryColor` under `theme: base` brings its text and border colors along. Renderizr reads `primaryColor`, `primaryBorderColor`, `primaryTextColor`, `lineColor`, `edgeLabelBackground`, `clusterBkg`, `clusterBorder`, `fontSize` and `fontFamily`, and on an ERD the [row colors](#erds). With no named theme they change Mermaid's `default` theme, which keeps its own node fill, as Mermaid does. In dark mode the palette keeps its fills, while edges and their labels, which draw straight on the canvas, take the color scheme's colors. `theme: dark` draws a dark palette in light mode too. | CSS | On a node | On an edge (`linkStyle`) | | --- | --- | --- | | `fill` | Its fill | | | `stroke` | Its border | The line's color | | `stroke-width` | The border's width | The line's thickness | | `stroke-dasharray` | A dashed border | A dashed line, unless the arrow syntax makes it dotted | | `color` | Its text | The label's text | | `font-size` | Its text size, in Mermaid's px | | | `font-weight` | Its name's weight, which is bold otherwise | | | `font-family` | Its family, ahead of the diagram's | | A subgraph's `style` and classes set its fill, border, text color and font size, and its border draws solid once the source sets a palette. A source fill keeps the border beneath it, as in Mermaid. A source's `curve` routes its edges: `linear` Direct, `step`, `stepBefore` and `stepAfter` Orthogonal, and every other curve Curved. # Contributing

This section takes you from a fresh clone to a merged pull request. Bug reports, feature requests and pull requests are all welcome on [GitHub](https://github.com/FormulaMonks/renderizr). Everyone taking part follows the [Code of Conduct](https://github.com/FormulaMonks/renderizr/blob/main/CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md). Report a security problem privately through [GitHub Security Advisories](https://github.com/FormulaMonks/renderizr/security/advisories/new), never as a public issue.

## Prerequisites

| Tool | Version | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Node | 22.13 or newer | pnpm 11 needs it. Renderizr itself runs on Node 20 or newer, and CI checks that floor with npm in a separate job |
| pnpm | 11 | The lockfile is `pnpm-lock.yaml`, and `pnpm-workspace.yaml` carries the build allow-list. npm and yarn drift the lockfile |
| git | any | To clone the repository |

Development runs on Node 24, which `.mise.toml` pins and `mise.lock` resolves. With [mise](https://mise.jdx.dev) installed, `mise install` in the repository root gets you the exact Node and pnpm the maintainers use. Any Node and pnpm that meet the table work too; nothing in the build reads mise.

## Get the code

```bash
git clone https://github.com/FormulaMonks/renderizr.git
cd renderizr
pnpm install
pnpm hooks
```

`pnpm hooks` installs the git hooks, once per clone. It stays a separate step because a `prepare` script runs whenever a package manager installs a package from a git URL, and `npx github:FormulaMonks/renderizr` does exactly that. Confirm the hooks took with `git config --get core.hooksPath`, which prints `.husky/_`.

### The test workspaces

The clone holds everything the tests need. The Big Bank plc, groups and Amazon Web Services workspaces the acceptance harness draws are unmodified copies from [structurizr/structurizr](https://github.com/structurizr/structurizr), committed under `test/__fixtures__/`. The repository keeps no submodule, because npm clones a git dependency with `--recurse-submodules`, and every cold `npx` would download it before the CLI starts.

[Reference](04-reference.md) covers the dev server and the build, every pnpm script, the project layout and where a new test goes.

## Branches and commits

Name every branch `<type>/<issue>/<short-description>`, for example `feat/42/resolve-view` or `fix/57/hash-routes-under-file`:

- `<type>` is `feat` for a new capability, `fix` for a bug and `chore` for everything else (docs, CI, refactors, dependencies and tooling).
- `<issue>` is the number of the GitHub issue the branch works on. Leave the segment out when the work has no issue: `chore/bump-biome`.
- `<short-description>` is a few lower-case words in kebab-case that say what the branch does.

Write commit messages as [Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org). The header reads `type(optional-scope): subject`, at most 100 characters, with a lower-case type and a subject that ends without a full stop. The types are `build`, `chore`, `ci`, `docs`, `feat`, `fix`, `perf`, `refactor`, `revert`, `style` and `test`. Mark a breaking change with `feat!:` or a `BREAKING CHANGE:` footer.

A maintainer squash-merges every pull request, so the pull request title becomes the commit that release-please reads. CI checks the title with the same commitlint rules.

### Git hooks

`pnpm hooks` installs three hooks from `.husky/`:

| Hook | Runs | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `prepare-commit-msg` | `pnpm exec czg --hook` | Opens an interactive prompt that writes the commit message when you pass no `-m` |
| `pre-commit` | `pnpm exec lint-staged` | Runs `biome ci` over the staged source files |
| `commit-msg` | `pnpm exec commitlint --edit` | Checks the message against Conventional Commits |

When `pre-commit` fails, run `pnpm format`, stage the files again and commit. When `commit-msg` fails, the output names the rule; run `git commit` again and let czg write the message. A per-clone switch turns each hook off, such as `git config custom.hooks.pre-commit false`, and `git config --unset` turns it back on. CI runs the same checks either way.

## Pull requests

Before you open one, run what CI runs:

```bash
pnpm lint
pnpm typecheck
pnpm test
```

Then build something real, as [Local development](04-reference.md#local-development) shows, and look at it in a browser. A rendering or documentation change that only passes the tests stays untested.

- **Keep one concern per pull request.** Branch off `main` and name the branch as [Branches and commits](#branches-and-commits) says.
- **Fill in the template**: what the change does and why, how a reviewer can see it work, and any additional notes. For anything visual, a screenshot before and after says more than a paragraph.
- **Test anything in `scripts/`.** New behavior gets a test, and a fixed bug gets the test that would have caught it.
- **Update the docs in the same pull request.** A new CLI flag changes `scripts/cli.js` and the flag table in the [usage section](02-usage.md#options).
- **Justify every new runtime dependency.** Everything in `dependencies` ends up inlined into a file people email around, so its weight needs a sentence of reasoning.
- **Open a draft** for work you want eyes on early, and mark it ready when CI passes.

## Reviews

CI runs lint, type checks, the test suite on Node 22 and 24, an npm install and build on Node 20, the end-to-end render and the pull request title check; CodeQL runs too. A maintainer reviews the pull request, usually within a week. Reviewers label each comment:

- **blocking**: change it before merge.
- **suggestion**: take it or explain why not; either answer merges.
- **nit**: cosmetic, never blocking.

Push fixes as new commits while a review is open, so reviewers can read the change since their last look. The ruleset on `main` requires a pull request with every review thread resolved and a passing `ci` check. Maintainers also wait for one approving review from someone other than the author before they merge.

## Releases

Contributors do nothing for a release. Consumers run `npx github:FormulaMonks/renderizr`, which resolves to `main`, so a merged pull request reaches users as soon as it lands.

[release-please](https://github.com/googleapis/release-please) keeps a release pull request open on `main` with the next version and its changelog entry, computed from the Conventional Commits since the last tag. Merging it tags the release and publishes the GitHub Release, with a source tarball, the fixture workspace rendered as a static site and as a single file, and checksums. Each release also renders `architecture/workspace.json` from its tag and publishes it to this site, so the site always shows the latest release. Nothing goes to a package registry.

# Reference

The details you look up while working on Renderizr: running it from a clone, every pnpm script, Structurizr's tools for edit mode, where the code lives and where a new test goes. [Contributing](03-contributing.md) covers the workflow around them.

## Local development

```bash
pnpm dev
```

Vite serves this repository's own workspace, `architecture/workspace.json`, on <http://localhost:5173>, with hot reload for `src/`. To check a change, point the dev server at a versioned fixture under `test/__fixtures__/` that shows it:

```bash
pnpm dev -- test/__fixtures__/edge-routing.json --font Inter
```

Always put `--` before the arguments. Without it, Vite reads them itself and stops on any option it does not know. The dev server accepts the branding flags `--logo <path|url>`, `--logo-alt <text>`, `--logo-href <url>`, `--font <family>` and `--primary-color <color>`, and `--single-file`, before or after the workspace path, and reads `RENDERIZR_WORKSPACE` from the environment when you pass no workspace. It takes the workspace's `renderizr.*` branding properties the way `pnpm render` does, and prints the same branding notices. Git tracks the fixtures, so `git status` shows whether anything changed one while you looked. When no fixture shows your change, add one in the same pull request.

To build what users get, run the production build:

```bash
pnpm render architecture/workspace.json --single-file
```

`pnpm render` runs `tsc` first, so a type error fails the build before Vite starts, then writes into `./structurizr-output` unless `--out` says otherwise. It takes its arguments with no `--`. Open `structurizr-output/index.html` in a browser to look at the result; a single file needs no server.

| `pnpm mermaid:parser` | Writes `scripts/mermaid/parser.js` again from Mermaid's source at the release `MERMAID_VERSION` pins, as [The Mermaid parser](#the-mermaid-parser) describes |
| `pnpm hooks` | Installs the git hooks, once per clone |
| `pnpm release:pr` | Opens or updates the release pull request with your own `gh` login, for maintainers |
| `pnpm release:tag` | Tags a merged release and creates its GitHub Release, for maintainers |

The script that renders a workspace is `render`, never `build`. npm prepares a git dependency with a full `npm install --include dev` whenever its `package.json` has a `build`, `prepare`, `prepack`, `install`, `preinstall` or `postinstall` script, and that slows every cold `npx` by seconds. `scripts/install.test.js` fails when one of those names comes back.

`pnpm architecture:merge` and `pnpm fixtures:acceptance` find Structurizr's tools the way [edit mode](#structurizrs-tools-for-a-dsl-session) does: `STRUCTURIZR_CLI` as a whole command, or `structurizr-cli` on the `PATH`.

Biome is the only linter and the only formatter. It indents with 4 spaces, skips `architecture/` and the workspaces copied from Structurizr, and respects `.gitignore`; `biome.json` holds the rest.

## Structurizr's tools for a DSL session

Renderizr never parses DSL. A DSL session runs Structurizr's own tools: `merge -workspace workspace.dsl -layout workspace.json`, which lays the saved layout over the model as Structurizr Local does, or `export` on the first run, while no `workspace.json` exists yet. Edit mode finds the tools in this order:

1. The `STRUCTURIZR_CLI` environment variable, read as a whole command.
2. `structurizr-cli` on your `PATH`.

The tools need Java 21 to 25; Groovy `!script` blocks fail on Java 26. Edit mode works with the 2026 distribution (`structurizr.war` and the `structurizr/structurizr` Docker image, where every tool is a subcommand) and with the archived `structurizr-cli` 2025.11.09.

```bash
STRUCTURIZR_CLI="java -jar ~/bin/structurizr.war" npx github:FormulaMonks/renderizr edit ./architecture
```

With Docker and no Java on your machine:

```bash
STRUCTURIZR_CLI='docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/usr/local/structurizr" structurizr/structurizr' npx github:FormulaMonks/renderizr edit ./architecture
```

Edit mode runs the command through the shell from the DSL's folder, so `$PWD` in single quotes expands there and the container mounts that folder. The tools write into a temporary `.renderizr-*` folder beside the DSL, which edit mode deletes after each run, and never write `workspace.json` themselves.

When a DSL change breaks the parse, the terminal prints the tools' output and the page shows the error over the last workspace that parsed, which stays editable. The next good run clears it.

Two behaviors come from Structurizr and stay as Structurizr has them:

- **The id fallback.** `merge` carries each element's position over by its canonical name and falls back to its id. When a DSL change renames an element and shifts the ids of others, `merge` can hand the renamed element another element's position. Check the views after a rename.
- **Unwatched includes.** Edit mode watches every file under the DSL's folder, except `workspace.json`, dot folders and `node_modules`. A file that `!include` pulls in from outside that folder goes unwatched, as in Structurizr Local: save a file inside the folder to run the tools again.

## Mermaid diagram notices

The build prints two kinds of notice about [Mermaid diagrams](02-usage.md#mermaid-diagrams), both on stderr, both naming the image view's key, and finishes either way. `pnpm dev` and edit mode print them to the terminal too.

A diagram Renderizr can't draw prints its reason, and the page shows the same text in place of the canvas: `Mermaid diagram "<key>": <reason>.`

| Reason | When |
| --- | --- |
| the image view carries no Mermaid source | A content field names the Mermaid server's `/svg/` or `/img/` path but holds nothing Renderizr can decode as text |
| a parse error at line N: … | Mermaid's own grammar stops on the source. The line counts from the top of the `.mmd` file, frontmatter included, and the message says what the parser stopped after |
| the content fields disagree | The image view fills more than one of `content`, `contentLight` and `contentDark`, and they hold different sources once CRLF becomes LF, or one holds a picture beside the Mermaid source |
| an edge to a subgraph isn't something Renderizr draws yet | An edge starts or ends at a subgraph. Such an edge carries meaning, so the build fails the whole diagram |
| the arrow end "…" isn't something Renderizr draws yet | An edge ends in a marker that matches no End marker. Renderizr draws a flowchart's arrows, circles and crosses |
| the cardinality "u" (parent) isn't something Renderizr draws yet | An ERD relationship ends in Mermaid's parent cardinality (`u\|`), which matches no End marker |
| an ERD subgraph isn't something Renderizr draws yet | An ERD groups entities in a `subgraph` |

A diagram that draws but uses what Renderizr leaves out prints one warning that lists it, each entry once, in this order: the config's entries, then the subgraphs' and nodes' (an ERD's entities), then the links', then the classes': `Image view "<key>": Renderizr supports only a subset of Mermaid styling; ignored: <entries>`.

| Entry | What Renderizr does instead |
| --- | --- |
| `theme "<name>"` | Draws Mermaid's `default` theme in place of a theme Mermaid doesn't know |
| `theme colors` | Draws the silent look when Mermaid's theme code can't read a theme variable's color, such as `#12345` |
| A theme variable, such as `mainBkg` | Derives the palette without a theme variable that [Styles](02-usage.md#styles) doesn't list, or on a sequence diagram that [Sequence diagrams](02-usage.md#sequence-diagrams) doesn't list |
| `look` | Draws Mermaid's `classic` look in place of `handDrawn` or `neo` |
| `htmlLabels` | Draws every label as plain text lines, whatever `htmlLabels` says; also named for a label that holds HTML, as Structurizr's `mermaid <viewKey>` writes it |
| `layout: elk` | Lays the diagram out with Dagre, since Renderizr doesn't bundle ELK |
| `elk.<option>` | Leaves out each ELK option |
| A CSS property, such as `opacity` | Leaves out a property that a node's or subgraph's `style`, a `classDef` or a `linkStyle` sets and that [Styles](02-usage.md#styles) doesn't list. A link's `fill:none` names nothing, since a line draws no fill |
| `shape "<name>"` | Draws a rectangle in place of a stadium, subroutine, asymmetric, parallelogram, trapezoid or double circle node, or of any other `@{ shape }` name |
| `invisible links` | Leaves each `~~~` link out of the drawing and the layout |
| `link length` | Lays a longer link (`--->`) out as an ordinary one |
| `Markdown strings` | Draws the text of a Markdown string without its emphasis |
| `fa: icons` | Draws a label without its Font Awesome icons |
| `click callbacks` | Leaves out a `click` line that calls a function (`click A callback`, `click A call notify()`); a `click` link still leads where it says |
| `curve` | Draws a sequence diagram's messages as straight lines, whatever `curve` says |
| `sequence.<text>FontSize`, `sequence.<text>FontFamily`, such as `sequence.actorFontSize` | Draws that sequence text at the size and in the family the top-level `fontSize` and `fontFamily` give |
| `messageMargin` | Spaces a sequence diagram's messages as Renderizr's layout does |
| `participant type "<type>"` | Draws a sequence diagram's `boundary`, `control`, `entity` or `collections` participant as the participant box |
| `half arrows` | Draws a sequence diagram's half arrow as a whole one at the end the syntax puts it: a solid half head as an arrow, a barb as an open arrow |

## The Mermaid parser

The build reads Mermaid source with `scripts/mermaid/parser.js`: Mermaid's own flowchart, ERD and sequence grammars and db classes, its frontmatter and directive reader and its theme code, cut loose from the rest of Mermaid and bundled into one ES module with Mermaid's MIT notice at the top. Only the build runs it; the page never carries it, and `mermaid` never enters Renderizr's dependencies.

`pnpm mermaid:parser` writes the file again. It checks out Mermaid's source at the tag that `MERMAID_VERSION` in `scripts/mermaid/generate/index.js` pins, installs its bundling tools into a folder of its own under the system's temporary folder, and bundles the reader with the stand-ins in `scripts/mermaid/generate/`. Two runs at one pin write the same bytes on any machine. It needs `git`, `npm` and the network.

Renovate raises the pin as a dependency update and never merges it on its own: run `pnpm mermaid:parser` on its branch, commit the parser it writes and check the Mermaid fixtures under `test/__fixtures__/` before it merges.

## Project layout

| Path | What lives there |
| --- | --- |
| `scripts/` | The build pipeline and edit mode's server, in plain ESM JavaScript that Node runs with no build step |
| `scripts/build.js` | The CLI entry point: checks the Node version, parses arguments, loads assets and runs Vite |
| `scripts/cli.js` | Option definitions and `--help`, for the build and for `renderizr edit` |
| `scripts/assets.js` | Fetching and embedding the workspace, themes, element icons, logo and font |
| `scripts/branding.js` | Choosing the branding from the flags and the workspace's `renderizr.*` properties, shared by the build, edit mode and the dev server |
| `scripts/edit.js`, `scripts/edit-plugin.js` | Edit mode: the session a path opens, the local server and its save endpoint |
| `scripts/dsl-pipeline.js`, `scripts/structurizr-tools.js` | Running Structurizr's tools on a `workspace.dsl` |
| `scripts/workspace-writer.js`, `scripts/structurizr-schema.js` | Writing `workspace.json` the way Structurizr does |
| `scripts/config.js` | The Vite configuration, shared with the dev server |
| `scripts/plugins.js` | Build plugins: branding injection and single-file inlining |
| `scripts/escapes.js` | Rewrites the escape sequences a Claude artifact upload rejects, and fails the build if any survive |
| `scripts/mermaid/` | Reading the Mermaid source an image view carries: decoding it, the generated parser and the plain model of each diagram the page draws |
| `vite.config.ts` | The dev server only; the production build goes through `scripts/build.js` |
| `src/` | The page that ships in the output, in TypeScript, bundled by Vite |
| `src/model/` | The typed workspace model and style resolution, ported from Structurizr, and `resolveView` |
| `src/engine/` | The React Flow engine: the diagram contract in `index.ts`, geometry, layout and the island |
| `src/pages/`, `src/components/` | The diagrams, documentation and decisions pages, and the parts they share |
| `test/` | Tests for `src/`, and the DOM and module hooks they run on in `test/support/` |
| `test/__fixtures__/` | Versioned workspaces for tests and for checking changes in the dev server |
| `architecture/` | Renderizr's own workspace, which this site renders |

The model layer in `src/model/` reads the workspace: a typed port of Structurizr's workspace model and style resolution, and `resolveView`, which turns any view key into a concrete view. `src/engine/geometry/` and `src/engine/layout/` are plain functions over that view: boundaries, shapes, unplaced elements, routes, and Dagre for automatic layout. The island in `src/engine/react-flow/` is a React root built on [React Flow](https://reactflow.dev) that draws the result inside the diagram target and nowhere else, and `src/engine/index.ts` is the only way in: `mountEngine` and the `Engine` it returns. The rest of the page stays plain TypeScript.

`scripts/` stays JavaScript and `src/` stays TypeScript. `tsconfig.json` includes only `src`, so the tests in `scripts/` are what guard the pipeline.

## Adding a test

Tests use the Node built-in runner. Put a test where its subject lives:

| Testing | Put it in | Import |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Anything in `scripts/` | `scripts/<module>.test.js`, next to the module | The module directly: `import { parseCliArgs } from "./cli.js"` |
| Anything in `src/` | `test/<subject>.test.js` | Through `test/support/ts.js`, which installs the DOM and the TypeScript hooks: `await importSrc("components/menu")` |

`pnpm test` picks up a new file ending in `.test.js` in either folder with nothing to register. `scripts/escapes.test.js` and `test/menu.test.js` are good models to copy.

The DOM in `test/support/dom.js` is a purpose-built subset, and its selector engine throws on any selector it does not implement. When valid CSS a component ships fails there, extend `dom.js` and add a case to `test/dom.test.js`. Timers and animation frames are fake: nothing deferred runs until a test calls `dom.runTimers()`.

`test/e2e.test.js` runs a real `--single-file` build in headless Chrome, and `test/acceptance.test.js` holds the engine's drawing of every acceptance view to the rules in `test/support/engine-checks.js`. Both skip themselves when the machine has no Chrome.
